# Circuit Archaeology: Excavating Hidden States, QK/OV Circuits, and the Machinery Inside a Transformer

## Two Weekends, Two Angles, One Question

There's an old line about understanding by building: you don't really know how something works until you've built it yourself. I took that literally, twice, from two different directions.

The first project, `transformers-anatomy-deep-dive`, was the "build it" half. No `AutoModel.from_pretrained()` shortcuts. I implemented the original Encoder-Decoder, BERT, and GPT from raw PyTorch, wrote the training loops by hand, and then actually pre-trained small versions of them so I could watch the loss curves, gradient norms, and internal representations evolve in real time.

The second project, `circuit-archaeology-transformer-circuits`, was the "take it apart" half. Instead of building a model, I loaded a real, pretrained GPT-2 into TransformerLens and went hunting for the actual circuits inside it: the QK and OV matrices, the residual stream geometry, the induction heads, following the roadmap laid out in Anthropic's *A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits*.

This post is the record of both weekends: what I built, what I measured, what matched the textbook story, and, more interestingly, what didn't.

## Before You Can Dissect a Frog, You Need to Build One

Before any circuit-hunting, I wanted a model I'd built with my own hands, verified line by line against a reference implementation. So the first thing `transformers-anatomy-deep-dive` does is rebuild GPT-2's architecture from scratch: tokenization, embeddings, causal masking, multi-head attention, the MLP block, the whole Pre-LayerNorm residual stack, and test every single module against a real, pretrained GPT-2 loaded through TransformerLens. LayerNorm, the embedding lookup, positional embeddings, the causal mask: each one passed its correctness test at 100% agreement with the reference model before I let myself move on.

Once I trusted the plumbing, I did the same thing for BERT, and I wanted a sanity check that was almost embarrassingly simple: can this model even learn? I took a fresh, randomly-initialized 12.8M-parameter mini-BERT (6 layers, 256 hidden dim, 8 heads) and asked it to fill in a masked sentence. Predictably, the untrained model produced nonsense, with words like "bethel," "lanterns," and "styled" standing in for whatever the actual missing word should have been. Then I did the oldest trick in the deep learning debugging book: overfit on a single example. One sentence, repeated for 100 epochs. Loss went from 10.48 down to 2.53. That's not a result anyone would publish, but it's the result that matters most: it's the proof that gradients are actually flowing through every layer, that nothing is silently dead. As a bonus, checking the gradient magnitudes by parameter group showed the token-type (segment) embeddings absorbing by far the largest average gradient (0.267, versus 0.0085 for the LayerNorm parameters), which makes total sense, since those embeddings start from scratch and have the most adjusting to do.

## Watching a Language Model Learn to Write Shakespeare

The more interesting pre-training run was a 6-layer, 384-dimensional, character-level GPT, about 0.82M parameters, trained on Tiny Shakespeare for 20,000 steps, with per-step logging of loss, residual stream norms, logit lens confidence, and gradient flow by component.

![Train vs. validation loss over 20,000 steps of nanoGPT pre-training on Tiny Shakespeare](data:image/png;base64,)

Both curves start right around the random-guess entropy for a 65-character vocabulary (ln 65 ≈ 4.17; the logged values were 4.21 train / 4.21 val) and fall steeply for the first 200 steps as the model picks up common bigrams and short words. By the end of training, train loss sat at 1.19 and validation at 1.48, a generalization gap of 0.29 that had been quietly widening the whole time, a small but honest signature of the model starting to memorize local training sequences rather than purely generalizing.

![Residual stream L2 norm evolution across training steps](data:image/png;base64,)

While that was happening, I was also logging the L2 norm of the residual stream at every layer, every 100 steps. Because of Pre-LayerNorm, growth here is expected to be sub-linear rather than exploding, since each layer normalizes its input before writing anything new, and that's roughly what the curves show: norms climb as the model learns to write meaningful (rather than random) vectors into the stream, then the growth rate settles down as training stabilizes.

![Logit lens maximum probability at the final token, tracked block-by-block over training](data:image/png;base64,)

The logit lens result is where things got genuinely surprising. Projecting each block's output through the final layer norm and the unembedding matrix, then tracking the model's peak confidence at the last token over the course of training, showed the *input* embedding and *Block 1* both racing to near-total confidence by the end of training (0.999 and 0.997 respectively). Block 2 followed closely at 0.984. But Block 3, right in the middle of this tiny 4-block network, never got past 0.41. Block 4 recovered somewhat, ending at 0.71. In a network this shallow, I expected something closer to monotonic improvement with depth. Instead, one middle layer looks like it never committed to a confident answer, even after 20,000 steps, a small, concrete example of how "deeper should mean more confident" is not a law of nature, just a tendency.

![Gradient norm trajectory by component, log scale, subsampled across training](data:image/png;base64,)

Breaking gradients down by component (embeddings, attention, FFN, LayerNorm) showed embeddings absorbing the largest and most volatile gradients throughout training: they're doing the heavy lifting of establishing token identity, while LayerNorm gradients stayed small and steady, consistent with their role as a stabilizer rather than a primary locus of learning.

![Distribution of gradient norms by component type](data:image/png;base64,)

And then, the fun part: actually reading what the model wrote after 20,000 steps.

> Considering grace, so young valiant yet so hold,
> To yield all him and see her makes a word good.
>
> SICINIUS:
> Sir, if I can disturb of this, well-say I saw it
> as himself with children of his mistress!

This is, structurally, uncannily correct Shakespeare, with capitalized character names followed by colons, blank lines between speakers, and stage-direction-shaped fragments like "Second Gentleman:". The vocabulary is real: "valiant," "villain," "commands," "grief," "tragic." Even the invented, non-words the model occasionally produces ("caff," "blody," "popinion") are phonotactically plausible fakes; the model has clearly learned which letter combinations *look* English even where it hasn't memorized the exact spelling of a rarer word. What it hasn't learned is anything longer-range: pronouns don't track a consistent referent, sentences are locally grammatical but globally meaningless, and there's no persistent thread connecting one line to the next. With only 6 layers and a context window that can meaningfully reach back maybe 40–60 characters, that ceiling is exactly what you'd predict. As I put it at the time: this is a successful mechanistic demonstration, not a failed generation.

## Full-Scale BERT: What 2.6 Million Tokens Can (and Can't) Teach a Masked Language Model

Alongside the character-level GPT, I ran a more "real" pre-training job: a 41.6M-parameter BERT, trained with proper masked-language-modeling on WikiText-2 (roughly 2.67M tokens), AdamW with a linear warmup and decay schedule, and mixed-precision training on a single T4.

| Epoch | Train Loss | Train Acc | Val Loss | Val Acc |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8.11 | 6.5% | 7.13 | 9.7% |
| 5 | 6.61 | 13.1% | 6.63 | 14.6% |
| 10 | 6.28 | 17.4% | 6.29 | 19.4% |

Both loss and accuracy move steadily and monotonically in the right direction across all 10 epochs, with train and validation curves staying close together the entire time, and there's no overfitting cliff here, mostly because there isn't enough data for the model to overfit *to*. I'll say the quiet part out loud, the same way I did in the notebook itself: with only ~2.6M tokens, this training run was never going to produce a BERT that does anything impressive at masked-word prediction. What it *does* show cleanly is a stable, correctly-converging pre-training loop: proof that the architecture, the masking procedure, and the optimizer are all doing their job. The ceiling here is data, not code.

## Switching Tools: From My Own Model to a Pretrained GPT-2

With hand-built models behaving the way the math said they should, the second project turned the question around: instead of building a small model and watching it learn, load a real, already-trained GPT-2-small into TransformerLens and go looking for the specific circuits responsible for specific behaviors.

GPT-2-small's numbers are worth having on hand, because almost everything below is a consequence of them: `d_model = 768`, 12 layers, 12 heads per layer, `d_head = 64`, vocabulary of 50,257 tokens, context length 1024.

The first thing I did with it was almost comically humbling: I fed the model a sentence *describing itself*, "This is the gpt2 small model that will be used to see the internal activations and qk and ov circuits", and asked it to predict each next token. It got 4 out of 24 right: "is," "be," "used," "the." Function words. Nothing about "qk" or "ov circuits" specifically, which is fair, since GPT-2 was never trained on mechanistic interpretability jargon. It's a good reminder that even a "good" language model's token-by-token accuracy on unfamiliar prose is mostly a story about predictable grammatical glue, not deep semantic understanding.

The second thing was a much more famous trick: feeding the model the string `"HookedTransformer"`, which its own tokenizer splits into `['H', 'ooked', 'Trans', 'former']`. The *first* time those four tokens appear in a prompt, there's no way to predict `'ooked'` after `'H'`; it's arbitrary. But if the string appears a second time later in the same context, the model correctly predicts `'ooked'`, `'Trans'`, and `'former'` in sequence, purely because it has seen the pattern `H → ooked → Trans → former` once already, earlier in the same context. That is a live induction head at work, and it was my cue to go build the tools to find it directly.

## The Residual Stream Is Not a Conveyor Belt

Everything in a transformer reads from and writes to one shared object: the residual stream, a `d_model`-dimensional vector at every token position that every attention head and every MLP adds its output back into. It's the "bus" the whole network runs on.

One number puts the whole architecture in perspective: each attention head only operates in a `d_head = 64`-dimensional subspace of that 768-dimensional stream, just 8.3% of the available bandwidth. And yet, across all 12 layers and 12 heads, the *total* attention compute dimension adds up to 9,216, twelve times the width of the bus itself. Every head is trying to read and write through a narrow window onto a channel that's shared with everyone else. That bottleneck is the residual stream's defining constraint, and a lot of what follows is really just tracing its consequences.

![Residual stream L2 norm at resid_pre, resid_mid, and resid_post across all 12 layers of GPT-2-small](data:image/png;base64,)

Tracking the residual stream's norm layer by layer (on the prompt "The cat sat on the mat and looked at the") showed attention consistently adding very little to the norm: the gap between `resid_pre` and `resid_mid` stays small throughout, while the MLP sublayer is doing most of the "writing." Growth is nearly flat through layer 8, then surges sharply in the final layers, with the last token position accumulating by far the largest norm by the end.

![Singular value spectra of the residual stream at layers 0, 3, 6, 9, and 11, plus variance-explained by rank](data:image/png;base64,)

Running an SVD on the residual stream matrix at each layer told an even stronger story. At layer 0, you need 5 components to explain 95% of the variance across token positions, reasonable since tokens are still mostly independent right after embedding. By layer 2, that number collapses to 1. It *stays* at 1 all the way through layer 9 or 10. A single direction is capturing essentially all of the token-level variance for eight layers in a row. Only at layer 11 does the effective dimensionality expand again, up to 4, with the network visibly branching back out just before projecting into vocabulary space.

![Frobenius-norm subspace overlap between the top singular directions of every pair of layers](data:image/png;base64,)

I checked whether that "single direction" is even the *same* direction across layers, by measuring the subspace overlap between every pair of layers' top singular vectors. Layers 2 through 10 all overlap with each other almost perfectly, the same dominant direction, established early and held essentially fixed for eight layers. Layer 1 is transitional (overlap around 0.47–0.50 with the mid-network block), and layer 11 breaks away sharply, overlapping only 0.38–0.42 with the middle layers and just 0.06 with layer 1, nearly orthogonal to where the network started.

I want to flag something here rather than smooth it over: a persistent rank-1 subspace for eight layers in a row sits awkwardly next to the *superposition* picture of transformers (Elhage et al., 2022), where the residual stream is supposed to be densely packing many nearly-orthogonal features rather than collapsing to one. My best guess is that this is partly an artifact of testing on one short, elevent-token prompt rather than a corpus; a longer, more varied input would likely need more directions to represent more independent facts about more tokens. I'm noting the tension rather than resolving it, because that's the honest way to report a surprising number.

![Logit lens metrics by layer: top-1 accuracy, entropy, true-token rank, and true-token probability](data:image/png;base64,)

The logit lens made the same point from a different angle. Projecting the residual stream through the final layer norm and the unembedding matrix at every layer, top-1 accuracy sits flat around 10% all the way through layer 10, then jumps to roughly 50% only at the very last layer. The rank of the true next token actually gets *worse* through the middle of the network before recovering sharply at the end, and probability mass on the correct answer stays noisy and low until it spikes at layer 11. I've started calling this the **Abrupt Decision Transition**: rather than gradually assembling a prediction layer by layer, the model appears to do most of its work in an internal, non-vocabulary-aligned geometry, and only forces that representation into token-space at the very last moment.

## A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits

Before going further into what I measured, it is worth making the framework itself precise. Everything that follows in this post rests on the account given by Elhage et al. (2021) in *A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits*, and the results only make sense in light of the algebra underneath them.

### The residual stream as a communication channel

Take a decoder-only transformer with $L$ layers, model dimension $d_{model}$, and a sequence of $n$ tokens. At every position $i$, the residual stream $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{model}}$ is initialized from the token and positional embeddings and then updated additively, layer by layer:

$$
x_i^{(l+1)} = x_i^{(l)} + \text{Attn}^{(l)}(x^{(l)})_i + \text{MLP}^{(l)}(x_i^{(l)} + \text{Attn}^{(l)}(x^{(l)})_i)
$$

Every attention head and every MLP reads from this same $d_{model}$-dimensional vector and writes back into it by simple addition. There is no separate channel per layer, no per-head private memory. This is the single structural fact the whole circuits framework is built on: because every component reads and writes through addition into one shared linear space, the entire network can be expanded into a sum of terms, one per path a piece of information could take from input to output. That expansion is what makes it possible to talk about individual "circuits" at all.

### Attention as a linear-algebraic operation

Within one attention head $h$, at layer $l$, the residual stream at each position is projected into three lower-dimensional subspaces via learned weight matrices $W_Q, W_K, W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{model} \times d_{head}}$:

$$
Q = X W_Q, \qquad K = X W_K, \qquad V = X W_V
$$

where $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{model}}$ stacks the residual stream across all $n$ token positions. The attention pattern, a distribution over source positions for every destination position, is computed as

$$
A = \text{softmax}\!\left( \frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d_{head}}} + M \right)
$$

with $M$ the causal mask ($M_{ij} = -\infty$ for $j > i$, $0$ otherwise), enforcing that a token can only attend to itself and to tokens before it. The head's contribution to the residual stream, before the output projection, is then the attention-weighted sum of value vectors, $A V$, projected back up to $d_{model}$ by $W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{head} \times d_{model}}$:

$$
\text{head}(X) = A(X) \, X W_V W_O
$$

This single equation already contains the entire QK/OV split. $A(X)$, the *pattern*, depends only on $W_Q$ and $W_K$. The *content* that gets moved, $X W_V W_O$, depends only on $W_V$ and $W_O$. These two computations do not interact: a head cannot use what it is about to write to decide where to look, because the pattern is computed first, independently, and only then applied to the value vectors. That independence is the whole reason it is meaningful to analyze $W_Q, W_K$ separately from $W_V, W_O$.

### The QK circuit

Define the composite matrix

$$
W_{QK} = W_Q W_K^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{model} \times d_{model}}
$$

Substituting $Q = X W_Q$ and $K = X W_K$ into the attention score gives

$$
Q K^\top = X W_Q W_K^\top X^\top = X \, W_{QK} \, X^\top
$$

so the raw attention score between a destination token $x_i$ and a source token $x_j$ can be written directly as a bilinear form in the residual stream itself:

$$
\text{score}(i, j) = \frac{x_i^\top W_{QK} \, x_j}{\sqrt{d_{head}}}
$$

$W_{QK}$ answers exactly one question: given the residual stream content at a destination position, which directions in the residual stream at a source position should raise the attention score? A head with strong positive weight along the "am I the previous token" direction of $W_{QK}$ will attend backward one step. A head with strong weight along a token-identity direction that matches the destination's own identity will produce a current-token pattern. This is why in the toy-model experiments below, current-token heads, previous-token heads, and attention-sink heads can be identified purely from the structure of $W_{QK}$, without ever looking at what the head writes.

### The OV circuit

The other half of the head is

$$
W_{OV} = W_V W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{model} \times d_{model}}
$$

Given a fixed attention pattern $A$, the head's net effect on the residual stream at destination $i$ is

$$
\text{head}(X)_i = \sum_j A_{ij} \, x_j^\top W_{OV}
$$

$W_{OV}$ answers the second question: once attention has decided to move information from source $j$ to destination $i$, what transformation gets applied to $x_j$ before it lands? Because $W_V$ maps $d_{model} \to d_{head}$ and $W_O$ maps $d_{head} \to d_{model}$, the composite $W_{OV}$ factors through a $d_{head}$-dimensional bottleneck and therefore has rank at most $d_{head}$, regardless of how large $d_{model}$ is. In GPT-2-small, with $d_{head} = 64$ and $d_{model} = 768$, every head's write operation is architecturally confined to a rank-64 subspace of a 768-dimensional space, a constraint that turns out to matter a great deal, and is exactly what the effective-rank measurements later in this post are measuring against.

### One head, one equation

Putting the two circuits back together, a single attention head's full contribution to the residual stream is

$$
\text{head}(X)_i = \sum_j \text{softmax}_j\!\left( \frac{x_i^\top W_{QK} x_j}{\sqrt{d_{head}}} \right) x_j^\top W_{OV}
$$

Everything a head does is contained in this expression: $W_{QK}$ inside the softmax controls *where*, $W_{OV}$ outside the softmax controls *what*. No other parameters are involved. Reading this equation is what it means, concretely, to treat a transformer as a circuit rather than as an opaque function: the model's behavior on any given input can be traced back to specific low-rank bilinear and linear maps acting on the shared residual stream.

### Multi-head composition and the residual stream bottleneck

A layer does not contain one head, it contains $n_{heads}$ of them, each with its own $W_Q^h, W_K^h, W_V^h, W_O^h$, all reading from and writing to the same residual stream in parallel:

$$
x_i^{(l+1)} = x_i^{(l)} + \sum_{h=1}^{n_{heads}} \text{head}^h(X^{(l)})_i
$$

Each head operates in its own private $d_{head}$-dimensional subspace ($64$ of $768$ dimensions in GPT-2-small, under 9% of the available space), but all heads across all layers write into the identical shared $d_{model}$-dimensional stream. This is the structural source of two things measured later in this post: the residual stream's total attention-compute dimension across all layers and heads vastly exceeding $d_{model}$ itself, forcing heavy reuse and compression of the space, and the destructive interference between layers, since nothing stops one head's write from partially cancelling another's.

Composition between heads across layers happens in exactly three ways, depending on which of the three matrices, $W_Q, W_K$, or $W_V$, reads output that an earlier head wrote:

- **Q-composition.** A later head's query is computed from a residual stream that an earlier head has already written into, so the earlier head influences *where* the later head looks.
- **K-composition.** A later head's key is computed from a residual stream an earlier head has written into, so the earlier head influences which source tokens the later head's queries will match against.
- **V-composition.** A later head's value is computed from a residual stream an earlier head has written into, so the earlier head influences *what content* the later head moves, independent of where it looks.

Induction heads are the canonical example of K-composition, and are the cleanest evidence that composition is a real, load-bearing mechanism rather than a theoretical possibility. A previous-token head in an early layer performs no interesting attention-pattern work of its own; its entire function is to copy the identity of token $x_{j-1}$ forward into the residual stream at position $j$. A later-layer induction head then computes its keys from *that* enriched residual stream. Because the key at position $j$ now effectively encodes "the token that came right before me," the induction head's query at the current position $i$, searching for "a position whose preceding token matches my current token," lights up precisely at the earlier occurrence of the current token, and copies whatever followed it. Neither head could produce this behavior alone; it is a genuinely two-layer, K-composed circuit, which is exactly why the ablation results later in this post show damage concentrated in both the previous-token head and the layer-1 heads simultaneously, and not in either alone.

## Induction Heads: Where QK and OV Actually Meet

Individual attention heads are interesting, but the first genuinely *algorithmic* behavior in a transformer, the first thing that looks less like a filter and more like a program, is the induction head, and it isn't implemented by a single head at all. It's a two-layer circuit: a **previous-token head** in an early layer that shifts token identity one position forward into the residual stream, and an **induction head** in a later layer that reads that shifted information (via what's called K-composition) to pattern-match the current token against its last occurrence, and copy whatever followed it.

To confirm the toy model actually had this circuit rather than just plausible-looking attention patterns, I ran the classic out-of-distribution stress test: feed the model a sequence of *random* tokens, repeated twice, `[A][B][C]...[A][B][C]`, and compare loss on the first half against the second. There's no way to do well on the first half; it's random. But if the model has learned the induction algorithm rather than memorizing training-data statistics, it should do dramatically better on the second half, purely by copying. That's exactly what happened:

![Model performance on the first vs. second half of a repeated random-token sequence](data:image/png;base64,)

Performance on the second half was dramatically better than the first, direct evidence that the model generalizes the repeat-and-predict pattern to sequences it has never seen, which is a much stronger claim than "the attention pattern looks like induction."

Scoring every head with an induction detector (checking attention mass at exactly the "one full repeat-length back" offset) flagged heads 1.4 and 1.10 as the strongest inducers, consistent with the diagonal band visible in their raw attention patterns. I then ran **direct logit attribution**, decomposing the correct-token logit into contributions from the direct embedding path and each individual attention head. On ordinary text, the biggest swings in the direct path lined up almost perfectly with the first half of common tokenizer bigrams ("manip" strongly predicting "ulative," "super" strongly predicting "human," "machine" predicting "learning"), a fun reminder that some of what looks like "prediction" is really just the tokenizer having split one conceptual unit into two pieces. On the repeated-random-token benchmark, the first half of the attribution plot was, appropriately, meaningless, since there's nothing predictable to attribute yet. But in the second half, heads 1.4 and 1.10 lit up exactly as expected.

Finally, to move from correlation to causation, I ran zero-ablation and mean-ablation over every head, measuring the increase in loss on the repeated-token benchmark when each head's output was surgically removed. Ablating head 0.7, the previous-token head identified earlier, did by far the most damage in layer 0, and the layer-1 heads flagged earlier as the strongest inducers were exactly the ones whose removal hurt the most in layer 1. That's the full circuit, confirmed three separate ways: by attention pattern, by logit attribution, and by causal ablation.

## Where the Textbook Story Started to Crack

![Cumulative per-layer contribution norms vs. actual residual stream norm, and the alignment between each layer's contribution and the running stream](data:image/png;base64,)

The last experiment I ran ties several of the threads above together, and it's the one that pushed back hardest against my initial mental model. If every layer just *adds* its contribution to the residual stream, the triangle inequality gives you an upper bound: the final norm should be at most the sum of the magnitudes of every individual layer's contribution. I computed that cumulative bound, roughly 1,100, and compared it against the residual stream's *actual* final norm: roughly 460. The gap is enormous: about 58% of the naive additive total simply isn't there. Layers aren't just stacking their contributions on top of each other; a large fraction of what they write is destructively cancelling against what's already in the stream.

Breaking the alignment between each layer's contribution and the running residual stream down by depth suggested a rough three-act structure: layers 0 to 3 behave like an **exploration** phase, establishing new candidate directions; layers 4–8 look like **consolidation**, deciding which of those directions to keep amplifying; and layers 9 to 11 behave like an **exploitation** phase, sharpening and boosting whatever survived for the final output. The residual stream, in other words, isn't a conveyor belt quietly carrying information from input to output. It's closer to a competitive arena where layers are constantly proposing, reinforcing, and cancelling each other's directions, and that ~58% cancellation gap is the visible cost of that competition.

## What I'd Dig Up Next

A few honest caveats, in the spirit of the project's own name, this is archaeology, and archaeology means admitting what you haven't excavated yet. Several of the most striking numbers here, the rank-1 mid-network collapse especially, came from single short prompts, not corpus-wide averages, and I'd want to see whether they hold up (or soften) once averaged over hundreds of varied inputs. The encoder-decoder half of the original Transformer architecture is scaffolded in `transformers-anatomy-deep-dive` but not yet trained end-to-end with cross-attention analysis, and that's the obvious next build. And the head-taxonomy detectors throughout are exactly what I called them at the time: heuristic, threshold-based hypotheses, not verified ground truth, and the natural next step is systematic, corpus-averaged ablation sweeps rather than single-prompt spot checks.

But the core method held up across both projects, and I think it's worth stating plainly: build the thing yourself first, verify it against a reference until you trust every module, and only *then* go looking for the circuits inside a model you didn't build. Some of what I found matched the textbook exactly: the QK/OV decomposition, the induction circuit, the MLP-dominated norm growth. And some of it didn't: the rank-1 highway through the middle of the network, the 58% cancellation gap, the attention-sink head hiding behind a misleadingly low rank. Both kinds of result were worth the weekend.
